Lignin is the most abundant natural aromatic feedstock, and the conversion of lignin to value-added chemicals has drawn immense attention in biorefineries. Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been used for lignocellulosic biomass fractionation and lignin extraction due to their simple procedure, selective solubility of lignin, low cost, and high recyclability. The nature and number of functional groups in DESs remarkably influence the delignification and structural changes of lignin during treatment. Although many studies have investigated lignin extraction and the following chemical transformations during DES treatment, no review has illuminated the structure-function relationships between DESs and lignin. This review presents a systematic overview of important studies to provide insights into lignin extraction and chemical transformations by examining the relationship between the type and number of functional groups in DES constituents during pretreatment. Furthermore, various challenges and opportunities in the development of more sustainable and efficient lignin extraction are provided according to the remaining problems in this field.

# 1 Introduction Due to the gradual depletion of fossil fuels and emerging environmental concerns, increasing attention has been paid to the development of alternative energy sources. Lignocellulosic biomass—mainly carbohydrates (cellulose and hemicelluloses) and lignin—is one of the most promising renewable feedstocks for producing chemicals and materials.1–3 Over the past several decades, carbohydrate fractions have been successfully converted into many valuable products, such as bioethanol, levulinic acid, and fermentable sugars, which have achieved commercial profitability.4–7 Biorefineries have widely utilized carbohydrate fractions, but significant amounts of lignin fractions remain underutilized.8,9 Thus, large-scale and high-value

Lignin is a complex, three-dimensional amorphous bio-polymer that is an abundant renewable aromatic resource.10 Its chemical structure is composed of phenylpropane units, derived from three monolignols, namely sinapyl alcohol (S), coniferyl alcohol (G), and p-coumaryl alcohol (H), which are linked by various types of ether bonds (C–O bonds) and carbon-carbon bonds.11 The use of lignin as a feedstock to prepare bio-based materials or to transform it into other chemicals has numerous advantages—it is the only natural aromatic feedstock and has high thermal stability and renew-ability.12 However, lignin upgrading has been hampered due to biomass recalcitrance, lignin structural heterogeneity, inefficient extraction of lignin from biomass, and undesired lignin condensation during biomass pretreatment.13,14 Therefore, an efficient fractionation process should enable the high-yield extraction and obtaining high-purity lignin, which is a key step towards realizing lignin valorization.

Traditional solvents for lignin extraction include dilute acids, alkali solvents, and organic solvents, which can solubilize lignin fragments (e.g., γ-valerolactone, tetrahydrofuran, and methanol). However, these solvents normally suffer from equipment corrosion, volatility, high toxicity, or the need for high temperatures and pressures, which may decrease commercial profitability. 15,16 Recently, ionic liquids (ILs) have

Despite being promising for lignin fractionation from ligno- cellulose, some disadvantages still restrict the practical appli- cations of ILs in biorefinery processes, such as their high costs, complex synthesis procedures, and poor recoverability.18,19 To overcome these limitations while retain- ing their desired features, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been investigated as novel green designer solvents.

DESs were first introduced by Abbott and co-workers and are eutectic mixtures that contain a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA). 21 Francisco et al. found that DESs can selectively solubilize large amounts of lignin and negligible amounts of cellulose, suggesting that they could be suitable for extracting lignin from ligno- cellulose. 22 DESs have shown promise for lignocellulosic biomass processing, including biomass pretreatment, carbo- hydrate product conversion, and lignin extraction and upgrading. 23-27 Yu et al. first applied microwave-assisted DES pretreatment to realize the ultrafast fractionation of com- ponents from biomass in 3 min. 28,29 Several previous works have focused on lignocellulose fractionation using various DES systems. 30-33 Readers can consult the review articles on the chemical processes intensification of lignocellulose fraction- ation and lignin extraction and upgrading using various DES systems. 34-38 However, there is no comprehensive understand- ing of the correlation between the lignin extraction efficiency and the structure and properties of DESs during lignocellulose pretreatment. Lignocellulose delignification and lignin struc-

ture transformation strongly depend on the properties and number of HBD/HBA functional groups in DESS. Elucidating the chemical transformation of lignin in DESs is needed to design effective DESs to extract lignin with tailored properties.

This review provides a comprehensive summary of related studies that have explored the relationships between the performance of DESs and lignin extraction from three aspects: (1) functional group type and number of HBDs, (2) various categories of HBAs, and (3) DESs incorporated with catalysts or additives. Moreover, the correlation between the Kamlet-Taft parameters of DESs and the efficiency of lignin extraction is reviewed. Finally, the structural transformations of lignin under different DES pretreatment conditions are systematically discussed, and viewpoints on the opportunities and challenges for green and efficient lignin extraction according to existing problems are also given. ## 2 Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) DESs are eutectic mixtures generally consisting of a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), which combine _via_ hydrogen bond (H-bond) interactions.39,40 H-bonds within the mixtures are responsible for charge delocalization; thus, the melting point of DESs is much lower than that of the individual components.41 For example, the mixture of ChCl (m.p. 302 °C) with urea (m.p. 132 °C) can lead to DESs with a melting point of 12 °C.42 DESs possess many merits, including the availability of raw materials, easy synthesis, tunable physicochemical properties, and good recyclability.43 DESs have been synthesized and used in different applications, such as catalysis, pharmaceutical applications, and biomass processing.44

Generally, DESs are classified into four main categories based on the nature of the complexing agent (Fig. 3). Type I DESs are formed from metal halides (e.g., AlCl3, AgCl, and CuCl3) and quaternary ammonium salts (e.g., choline chloride (ChCl), and have not been significantly applied to ligno-cellulose processing owing to the high melting points of non-hydrated metal halides.39 Type II DESs mainly include hydrated metal halides (e.g., AlCl3.6H2O) and ChCl, which are more viable for industrial processes because most of these chemicals are low cost and are inherently insensitive to air/moisture. Type III DESs mainly consist of ChCl and various HBDs, such as carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amides. Type IV DESs include inorganic transition metals and HBDs (e.g., urea), even though metal salts do not normally ionize in non-aqueous media.45 Among the four types of DESs, Type III is the most common (especially in biomass processing), due to their low-cost starting materials, easy preparation, interactivity with water, low viscosity, and high biodegradability.37,46

chemical properties of DESs is essential to fractionate lignin from lignocellulose. The important properties of DESs include the melting point, viscosity, conductivity, density, polarity, and surface tension. One of the important features of DESs is that they possess a lower melting point than their individual con- stituents, which is responsible for the charge delocalization due to the formation of H-bonds between HBAs and HBDs.39 Hence, most DESs with low melting points exist as liquids at room temperature, allowing them to be used as solvents in biomass processing. In general, the melting point of DESS decreases upon increasing the H-bonding strength between mixtures.47 However, the presence of extensive H-bonding net- works within a mixture may increase the viscosity of DESS. Numerous studies have revealed that DESs with high viscos-
ities are unfavorable for lignin extraction due to the low rates of heat and mass transfer during DES pretreatment.⁴³

The high viscosity of DESS still poses a problem. Conductivity and surface tension are closely related to viscosity. 43,48 It has been reported that reducing the viscosity of DESs can promote its conductivity. 49 Moreover, the conduc- tivity of DESs is inversely proportional to temperature. 50 In most cases, DESs have higher surface tensions than many con- ventional ILs.51 The presence of water and low temperature can enhance the surface tension of DESS. 52 The surface tension of DESs strongly depends on the intermolecular forces between mixtures; thus, highly viscous DESs are fluids with high surface tensions. 53 Density also is an important property of DESs, as it can reveal the activity and molecular mobility of the solution. This information is helpful in some applications like lignin extraction processes. In most cases, DESs have a higher density than water. 37,53 It is generally observed that increasing the temperature or adding water to DESs lowers their density. 53-55 Overall, the understanding of the prepa- ration, classification, and physiochemical properties of DESS facilitate their utilization in lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin extraction.

Accordingly, the DESs are able to act either as hydrotropes or cosolvents to improve the lignin solubilization.⁵⁸ The DES per- formance in lignin extraction is affected by many factors, such as pretreatment time, extraction temperature, DES type, solid- to-liquid ratio, and HBA/HBD mole ratio. Among these factors, the quality and quantity of functional group in DES com- ponents have the greatest influence. The DESs are usually pre- pared by mixing natural and renewable constituents, which determines the properties of the synthetic DESs and their be- havior during lignin fractionation from biomass.

3.1 Functional group type and number in HBDs Many HBDs including carboxylic acids, polyols, and amides are suitable for DES synthesis. The functional group of HBDs can interact with lignin, which affects the lignin extraction efficiency and chemical structure. Investigating the relationships between the types of functional groups in HBDs and lignin extraction is important to produce DESs to extract lignin with tailored properties. In addition, depending on the number of functional groups (e.g., carboxyl groups) in HBDs, the lignin extraction yield has been reported to vary (Fig. 4).

3.1.1 Carboxyl-containing HBDs. Numerous HBDs with carboxyl groups exhibit better performance in biomass pre-treatment and delignification than those containing other groups (e.g., hydroxyl groups), regardless of the HBA used. Carboxyl-containing HBDs are more diverse, including formic acid, oxalic acid, and lactic acid, and most can remove >90% lignin from nearly all types of lignocellulose (poplar, Douglass fir, grass, and willow) when the molar ratio of HBD to HBA is high.²³,²⁸,⁶³,⁶⁴ This excellent delignification capacity mainly arises due to the presence of more active protons supplied by carboxylic acids, which promotes the proton-catalyzed cleavage

To further understand the influence of various carboxyl-con- taining HBDs on the performance of DESs, it is necessary to explore the structure-function relationships of various car- boxyl-containing DESs.

The properties of carboxylic acid-based HBDs can affect the performance of DESs during lignin extraction. Previous research has shown that the lignin extraction ability improves with the acid strength of HBD. The acid dissociation constant (pKa) of monocarboxylic acid-based DESs increases in the order: ChCl/formic acid, ChCl/lactic acid, ChCl/acetic acid, ChCl/butanoic acid, and ChCl/propionic acid, while the lignin extraction performance generally decreases. 59 However, ChCl/ lactic acid (pKa = 3.86) produced a greater pretreatment effect than a stronger acid, ChCl/malonic (pKa₁ = 2.83, pKa₂ = 5.69).63 However, ChCl/malonic acid exhibited a better deligni- fication performance from rice straw than ChCl/oxalic acid (pKa₁ = 1.25, pKa₂ = 4.14).60 These results implied that the lignin fractionation efficiency was not necessarily related to the amount or strength of the acid when the HBD contained more than one carboxyl group.

The number of carboxyl groups in an HBD is positively correlated with the extent of delignification during DES pretreatment. ChCl/lactic acid (1:9 molar ratio) (a monocarboxylic acid) is capable of selectively dissolving 95% of lignin from poplar and achieving higher lignin extraction yield than ChCl/succinic acid (a dicarboxylic acid) and ChCl/citric acid (a tricarboxylic acid).65 The result indicated that the monocarboxylic acid HBD possessed the optimal extraction capacity compared with the di- and tricarboxylic acids. This finding agrees well with Tan et al., who showed that the lignin extraction efficiency declined as follows: ChCl/lactic acid > ChCl/malic acid > ChCl/citric acid at the same molar ratio.59 One possible explanation for the weak delignification of di- and tricarboxylic acids is that the carboxyl groups in the HBD may easily be activated and thus release carbon dioxide at relatively high temperatures.63 The study also found that extra carboxyl groups in HBDs formed more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, which reduced the mass transfer rate of the solvent system.66 This implied that efficient interactions between DESs and lignins were impaired when there was more than one carboxyl group in the HBD. Hence, the number of carboxyl groups in HBDs is inversely proportional to the delignification ability of the DESs.

3.1.2 Hydroxyl-containing HBDs. HBDs with hydroxyl groups are also widely used to synthesize DESs, including poly-alcohol-based HBDs (e.g., ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, and glycerol) and carbohydrate-based HBDs (e.g., glucose, fructose, and xylitol).67,68 This type of DES usually exhibits good biocompatibility with enzymes and microorganisms at near-neutral pH when mixed with a nontoxic HBA (e.g., betaine, ChCl). Due to the neutrality of the hydroxyl-containing HBDs, most works have shown that polyalcohols or carbohydrate-based DESs have low efficiencies during lignin dissolution and fractionation, even under severe pretreatment conditions.

Hydroxyl-containing HBD pretreatment is suitable for grass, which has a weaker bond energy of the covalent bond. 23,69,70 Hydroxyl groups in HBDs play a positive role during lignin extraction. Compared with the performance of DESs with the same number of carboxyl groups, ChCl/lactic acid (C3H6O3) with a 33.5% lignin yield outperformed ChCl/propionic acid (C3H6O2) with 20.4% and ChCl/malic acid (C4H6O5) achieved a higher lignin yield (22%) than ChCl/succinic acid (C4H6O4) (6%). 59 Therefore, the presence of hydroxyl groups in HBDs improves the performance of DESs during lignin extraction, due to interactions between the hydroxyl groups in the HBD and the free and etherified hydroxyl groups in lignin. Therefore, exploring how the hydroxyl groups in HBDs affect the performance of DESs will help improve pretreatment by DESs.

The number of hydroxyl groups in HBDs is inversely corre-lated with lignin removal. ChCl/glycerol showed worse lignin extractability than ChCl/ethylene glycol. 63,65 In another work, the pretreatment efficiency and lignin removability of polyalco-hol-based DESs decreased in the order of ethylene glycol > gly-cerol > xylitol for polyol sequences when using lactic acid as the HBA. 60 Therefore, during DES pretreatment, a lower delignification rate was associated with a higher number of hydroxyl groups in the HBD. It was deduced that the extra hydroxyl groups in HBDs formed an extensive H-bond network between HBAs and HBDs, thus weakening the ability of the HBA to compete with intra-molecular bonding in the biomass components.71 With the same number of hydroxyl groups in different positions, the delignification ability was also slightly different. For example, ChCl/1,3-propanediol separated more lignin from rice straw than ChCl/1,2-propanediol. 60 The author showed that the greater hydrophobicity of 1,3-propanediol-based DESs promoted lignin extraction using the hydrophobic phenylpropanoid skeleton.

3.1.3 Amine/amide-containing HBDs. To further under- stand the effect of functional groups in HBDs on the perform- ance of DESS, HBDs with amine/amide groups, such as urea, imidazole, and ethanolamine, were explored for their lignin fractionation effects. For instance, corncob pretreated by ChCl/ imidazole at 150 °C removed 88% of lignin.72 Amines or amides present in HBDs improved lignin extraction by DESS, due to the loosened linkages between lignin and carbo- hydrates. A common feature of amine/amide-based DESs is their basicity, which is conducive for the extraction of lignin from lignocellulose. As the basicity decreased from ChCl/ monoethanolamine, ChCl/diethanolamine, ChCl/ N-methyldiethanolamine, to ChCl/urea, the lignin removal rate significantly decreased from 81.0%, 73.5%, 44.6%, to 27.7%, respectively.73 The main reason for this trend was that the phe- nolic hydroxyl groups of lignin were deprotonated in alkaline solutions. In addition, the effect of the number of amine groups in the HBD on the lignin removal ability was also inves- tigated to improve pretreatment efficiency. Lactic acid/forma- mide achieved a higher lignin removal rate from rice straw than lactic acid/urea,60 which implied that the pretreatment performance of amine/amide-based HBDs showed an identical

trend to hydroxyl-containing HBDs. HBDs with extra amines/ amides or hydroxyls can form more intermolecular H-bonds with HBAs, which reduces the number of free and active groups capable of interacting with lignocellulose and lowers the lignin production efficiency during DES pretreatment.

3.1.4 Alkyl chain length of HBD. Few investigations have been conducted on the relationship between the aliphatic chain length and lignin extractability, although initial research suggests that the alkyl group position in the HBD appears to affect the lignin extraction efficiency. Methyldiethanolamine (44.6%) containing an alkyl group (methyl) showed a weaker lignin fractionation ability than diethanolamine (73.5%).73 The main cause was the likely steric hindrance from the methyl group in methyldiethanolamine, which hampered the lignin fractionation efficiency. Moreover, the alkyl chain length of the HBD also influences lignin extraction. For monocarboxylic HBDs, the extracted lignin yield decreased as follows: ChCl/formic acid (62%) > ChCl/acetic acid (27%) > ChCl/propionic acid (20%) > ChCl/butanoic acid (14%) (Fig. 5).59 For dicarboxylic HBDs, the lignin extraction rate decreased as follows: ChCl/oxalic acid (98.5%) > ChCl/malonic acid (56.5%) > ChCl/glutaric acid (34.3%).63 Overall, HBDs containing shorter alkyl chains were more effective at delignification than those with longer chains, possibly due to electron donation from the alkyl group to the oxygen of the -OH group in the acid, which intensified the H-bonding strength.74 Weaker acids ionize to a lesser extent; therefore, decreasing the chain length of the HBD will increase the ability of the solvent to donate protons, which improves the DES pretreatment performance. However, another research study has found that ChCl/lactic acid (C3H6O3) produced a higher delignification efficiency than ChCl/glycolic acid (C2H4O3) when pretreated under the same conditions.60 It is likely that intramolecular H-bonds between adjacent functional groups in glycolic acid formed more easily than those in lactic acid, which made it difficult to cleave the various bonds in lignin. More efforts should be made to further understand the relationship between the alkyl chain length in HBDs and the lignin removal rate.

3.1.5 Lignin-derived HBDs. Numerous lignin-derived phenolic compounds, such as resorcinol, vanillin, and catechol, have been evaluated as HBDs for synthesizing DESs in biomass pretreatment. ## 3.2 Categories of HBAs HBAs also play important roles in the pretreatment perform-ance of DESs. The lignin extraction performance of ChCl/ formic acid was compared with that of pure formic acid, and the results showed that ChCl/formic acid removed 40.7% of lignin, while pure formic acid only removed 9.0% from herbal residues. 79 Hence, the DESs display better lignin fractionation than the corresponding acids alone. The high efficiency of DES delignification is attributed to the synergistic effects of HBDs and HBAs. 80 Currently, HBAs mainly include a variety of ammonium, phosphonium, and sulfonium salts.39 One of the most widespread HBAs for synthesizing DESs is ChCl, due to its biodegradability, low cost, and nontoxicity. Previous research has found that the highly electronegative Cl⁻ in ChCl tended to form H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups in lignin, which improved lignin removal.81 Other research studies have shown that the halide counterion in the HBA facilitates the breakage of β-O-4' bonds and also prevents lignin self-condensation. 82,83 However, when containing the same halogen ions, betaine-based DESs only dissolved 12% lignin at the same substrate loading, while ChCl-based DESs dissolved 100% of lignin. 84 This implies that the efficiency of lignin removal is closely influenced by the coordinating ability of cations in the HBA. # 4 Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic parameters of DESs Although a variety of DESs has been synthesized, there are no systematic studies on the relationship between DES properties and industrial applications. The chemical properties of DESs can be described by the Kamlet–Taft (K–T) solvatochromic parameters, which serve as a quantitative tool.⁹⁹ The K–T parameters are defined by three solvent parameters, including H-bond-donating ability (α), H-bond-accepting ability (β), and polarizability (π*). These parameters can be used to explain the internal connections between DES properties and their ability to fractionate lignin from lignocellulose.²³ For example, Yu et al. studied the correlations between the K–T parameters of DESs and the lignin extraction rate and found that the β value was positively correlated with the delignification rate.⁷¹ The authors explained that a high H-bond basicity improved the ability of the DES to break the H-bond network in lignin. In another work, ChCl/oxalic acid with a high H-bond acidity (α = 1.31) broke the structure of the lignin–hemicellulose complex, while ChCl/urea and ChCl/glycerol did not.²⁸ This is because the acidic protons dissociated from DESs catalyzed the cleavage of ethers and esters in lignocellulose. Moreover, the lignin-dissolving ability was related to the difference between the values of α and β (α–β), which shows a net H-bond-donating ability of DESs. For example, the lignin solubility/extraction capability of DESs increased at higher α–β values.⁸⁵,¹⁰⁰ These results imply that DESs with high α–β values could form strong H-bonds with lignin, which was favorable for the degradation of lignin. In addition to α and β values, the π* value of DESs also affects the lignin extraction ability. Studies have shown a close correlation between lignin extraction/solubility and π* values;²³,¹⁰¹ however, there is still a lack of a systematic overview for specific interactions between lignin extraction and the K–T parameters of DESs.

To understand which of the three parameters (α, β, and π*) is most important for delignification, the correlation between the K-T parameters and lignin extraction rate are summarized based on the existing data (Fig. 9). It was observed that the relationship between the lignin extraction ability and the K-T parameters varied depending on DES composition. # 5 Chemical transformation of lignin during DES pretreatment Due to the good performance of DESs in achieving high enzymatic saccharification yields and delignification from lignocellulose, the mechanisms about the interaction of DESs with lignin have recently gained more attention. For ChCl-based DESs, chloride anions are capable of forming strong H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups of lignin fragments, which break the intramolecular H-bond network of lignin and promote lignin fractionation.71 C-H···π and O···H bonding interactions contributed to the high interaction energy between ChCl/lactic acid and lignin, thus enhancing lignin dissolution in DESs.102 An insight into the structural transformations of lignin during DES pretreatment is not only essential to understand and overcome biomass recalcitrance but it is also pivotal to design optimal pathways for lignin valorization. During DES processing, both depolymerization and repolymerization can occur; thus, the final structure of the DES-extracted lignin may be the net effect of the two reactions whose outcome strongly depends on the processing method, which includes: (1) acidic DES pretreatment, (2) alkaline DES pretreatment, and (3) neutral DES pretreatment. This following section summarizes the possible chemical reactions during DES pretreatment, with
a focus on the fate of β-O-4' linkages in the lignin substructure.

## 5.1 Acidic DES pretreatment Acidic DESs exhibit excellent performance during lignin extraction; thus, investigation into the structural transformations of lignin in acidic DESs is necessary for lignin valorization. The possible reactions of the lignin substructure during acidic DES pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 10. The main reaction is lignin depolymerization, especially the breakage of β-O-4' bonds. Alvarez-Vasco et al. have reported that when treated with ChCl/lactic acid, guaiacylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (a β-O-4' bond lignin dimeric model compound) got converted into guaiacol and Hibbert's ketone.²³ This result demonstrated that the breakage of β-O-4' bonds favored lignin depolymerization, which consequently facilitated lignin fractionation from lignocellulose. Similar research also proved that acidic DESs can selectively cleave ethers and degrade a small portion of C-C bonds (e.g., β-5' and β-β') in lignin, which facilitates lignin separation from lignocellulose.⁶⁵,¹⁰³ The prevailing depolymerization pathway during acidic DESs is the destruction of the β-O-4' linkages among phenylpropane units via mild acid-catalyzed bond cleavage.²³,³⁴,¹⁰⁰,¹⁰⁴ The most important step is the protonation of the α-OH group to form a stable benzylic carbocation. Then, the benzylic carbocation loses the terminal γ-CH₂OH group to generate α-β unsaturated compounds and formaldehyde, which further promotes the cleavage of ether bonds (Route I). The subsequent hydrolysis of the acid-labile enol ethers causes the breakage of the β-O-4' bonds, followed by the modification of the Hibbert's ketone moiety in DES systems, finally producing depolymerized compounds, such as monoketone and diketone compounds (Route II). Another pathway is the allylic rearrangement of an enol ether intermediate followed by hydrolysis, which leads to the cleavage of β-O-4' bonds and produces monoketone and diketone compounds (Route III). During acidic DES pretreatment, without an interacting anion, it proceeds through Route I with the elimination of formaldehyde; when the DES anion (halide ion) interacts with the γ-OH group, Route II and III are favored, similar to dilute acids and acidic ILs. 105-107 Certain acidic DESs oxidize the α-OH group, followed by the acylation of the γ-OH group, which favors ether bond cleavage to yield diketones (not depicted in Fig. 10). 100,108 It is worth noting that lignin depolymerized products in DES systems contain diketone compounds, which have not been found in other acid pretreatments up to now.

In addition to depolymerization, repolymerization of lignin fractions can also occur during acidic DES pretreatment. For example, Shen and co-workers found that the chemical shift of the guaiacyl unit of lignin changed after ChCl/lactic acid pro- cessing, which suggested the formation of new C–C bonds via acid-catalyzed recondensation. 109,110 Repolymerization com- monly occurs through the formation of covalent bonds between the α-C of the benzylic carbocation and electron-rich positions on aromatic rings to obtain diphenylmethane com- pounds. However, the coupling between the electrophilic posi- tions on the aromatic rings of benzylic carbocations and elec- tron-rich positions of aromatic rings forms biphenyl com- pounds. Acidic DESs not only result in the condensation of

lignin fraction (e.g. ChCl/lactic acid) but also preserve lignin from condensation and produce non-condensed lignin (e.g., ChCl/boric acid). Non-condensed lignin was reported by Hiltunen's groups, with softwood sawdust as the raw material and ChCl/boric acid as the pretreatment solvent at 95 °C.111 The reason for the production of non-condensation lignin is that boric acid, a Lewis acid, can form esters with side-chain hydroxyl groups in lignin, thus reducing oligomerization and repolymerization reactions.

In certain acidic DES systems, esterification occurs between carboxyl groups in acidic DESs and y-OH in lignin substruc- tures. Several research groups have reported that y-acetylated signals in DES-extracted lignin were observed by 2D-HSQC NMR (Fig. S1†), which indicated the acylation of lactic acid during ChCl/lactic acid pretreatment. 65,82,100,109 In addition to the above reactions, demethoxylation and dehydration also fre- quently occur during DES pretreatment. 100,110 However, the exact mechanism is complex and not clearly understood.

## 5.2 Alkaline DES pretreatment Alkaline solvents are often used to extract lignin from biomass because lignin is an alkaline-soluble biopolymer.107 For example, chemical fractions of holocellulose, α-cellulose, and acid-insoluble lignin were pretreated with ChCl/urea, and lignin exhibited a higher selective solubility compared with other chemical fractions.112 Alkaline DES pretreatment destroys lignin-carbohydrate compounds, disrupts lignin by breaking the ether bonds, and eventually results in lignin depolymerization/repolymerization.97 Similarly, pretreatment with basic ILs resulted in the cleavage of ether bonds, along with demethoxylation, dehydration, and repolymerization primarily through β-β'and β-5' linkages.113 In another study, basic

## 5.3 Neutral DES pretreatment In contrast to acidic and alkaline DES pretreatment, neutral DES pretreatment has a minor effect on lignin extraction and structural transformation. Yu et al. revealed that the intramolecular H-bonds in ChCl/glycerol were mutually constrained by anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]⁻) and cationic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺), in which ChCl/glycerol had weakly competing interactions towards the linkages in the network of the lignin-carbohydrate complex.⁷¹ Wan and co-workers showed that lignin recovered from ChCl/glycerol pretreatment partially preserved the β-O-4' linkages and had a similar structure to protolignin.⁶⁹ In another study, the lignin extracted after ChCl/ethylene glycol pretreatment exhibited a low molecular weight and preserved partial β-O-4' bonds;⁸⁷,¹¹⁶ however, few studies have

examined the lignin transformation mechanism using alkaline DESs. After near-neutral IL pretreatment, lignin possessed the highest β-O-4' content, the largest molecular weight, and the minimum degree of condensation compared to that after acidic/basic IL pretreatment;¹¹⁴ therefore, pretreatment with neutral DESs may only slightly change the lignin structure. However, a comprehensive study of the structural transformation of lignin in neutral DES systems is required.

# 6 Conclusions and prospects The applications of DESs for lignin extraction and conversion have been widely recognized. Although a variety of DESs has been widely studied and used in biomass pretreatment, there is still a need for a rigorous investigation on the structure-function relationship of DESs during processing to increase the pretreatment efficiency. The properties of ideal DESs for lignin extraction are still unclear. Research on DES synthesis and its practical applications are still in their infancy, and thus more in-depth studies are required to increase DES pretreatment efficiency in future works. To achieve the ultimate goal of efficient lignin extraction and upgrading in terms of depolymerization and functionalization, there is still much work to do, as follows:

(1) DESs are ideal solvents for lignin fractionation and cata-lytic upgrading. Nevertheless, most DES screening methods are based on time-consuming trial and error. The directed design of DESs based on their intended purpose is promising. Besides, if lignin-derived compounds can be further used to synthesize DESs, a promising approach may be opened up to utilize lignin.

Systematic studies concerning how the K-T solvatochromic parameters of DESs affect lignin extraction are important, but so far only a few studies have investigated this topic. (3) Although various DESs have been widely applied in lignocellulose pretreatment, previous work has revealed that DES selectivity and lignin extraction yield vary greatly in different DES systems. Investigating the properties of DESs is vital to ensure their feasibility for lignin extraction and elucidating the interactions between DESs and lignin will greatly improve lignin extraction and valorization. (4) Traditional DES pretreatment processes carry out lignocellulose fractionation and conversion separately, which significantly increases the operating costs, the number of process operational steps, and waste discharge. Hence, it is necessary to develop a novel DES pretreatment technology that integrates lignin fractionation, enzymatic saccharification, and fermentation in a single vessel. Moreover, effective DES recycling methods should be investigated.

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been used for lignocellulosic biomass fractionation and lignin extraction due to their simple procedure, selective solubility of lignin, low cost, and high recyclability. The nature and number of functional groups in DESs remarkably influence the delignification and structural changes of lignin during treatment. Although many studies have investigated lignin extraction and the following chemical transformations during DES treatment, no review has illuminated the structure-function relationships between DESs and lignin. This review presents a systematic overview of important studies to provide insights into lignin extraction and chemical transformations by examining the relationship between the type and number of functional groups in DES constituents during pretreatment. Furthermore, various challenges and opportunities in the development of more sustainable and efficient lignin extraction are provided according to the remaining problems in this field. # 1 Introduction Due to the gradual depletion of fossil fuels and emerging environmental concerns, increasing attention has been paid to the development of alternative energy sources. Lignin is a complex, three-dimensional amorphous bio-polymer that is an abundant renewable aromatic resource.10 Its chemical structure is composed of phenylpropane units, derived from three monolignols, namely sinapyl alcohol (S), coniferyl alcohol (G), and p-coumaryl alcohol (H), which are linked by various types of ether bonds (C–O bonds) and carbon-carbon bonds.11 The use of lignin as a feedstock to prepare bio-based materials or to transform it into other chemicals has numerous advantages—it is the only natural aromatic feedstock and has high thermal stability and renew-ability.12 However, lignin upgrading has been hampered due to biomass recalcitrance, lignin structural heterogeneity, inefficient extraction of lignin from biomass, and undesired lignin condensation during biomass pretreatment.13,14 Therefore, an efficient fractionation process should enable the high-yield extraction and obtaining high-purity lignin, which is a key step towards realizing lignin valorization. Traditional solvents for lignin extraction include dilute acids, alkali solvents, and organic solvents, which can solubilize lignin fragments (e.g., γ-valerolactone, tetrahydrofuran, and methanol). Despite being promising for lignin fractionation from ligno- cellulose, some disadvantages still restrict the practical appli- cations of ILs in biorefinery processes, such as their high costs, complex synthesis procedures, and poor recoverability.18,19 To overcome these limitations while retain- ing their desired features, deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have been investigated as novel green designer solvents. DESs were first introduced by Abbott and co-workers and are eutectic mixtures that contain a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA). 21 Francisco et al. found that DESs can selectively solubilize large amounts of lignin and negligible amounts of cellulose, suggesting that they could be suitable for extracting lignin from ligno- cellulose. 22 DESs have shown promise for lignocellulosic biomass processing, including biomass pretreatment, carbo- hydrate product conversion, and lignin extraction and upgrading. 23-27 Yu et al. first applied microwave-assisted DES pretreatment to realize the ultrafast fractionation of com- ponents from biomass in 3 min. 28,29 Several previous works have focused on lignocellulose fractionation using various DES systems. 30-33 Readers can consult the review articles on the chemical processes intensification of lignocellulose fraction- ation and lignin extraction and upgrading using various DES systems. 34-38 However, there is no comprehensive understand- ing of the correlation between the lignin extraction efficiency and the structure and properties of DESs during lignocellulose pretreatment. Lignocellulose delignification and lignin struc- ture transformation strongly depend on the properties and number of HBD/HBA functional groups in DESS. Elucidating the chemical transformation of lignin in DESs is needed to design effective DESs to extract lignin with tailored properties. This review provides a comprehensive summary of related studies that have explored the relationships between the performance of DESs and lignin extraction from three aspects: (1) functional group type and number of HBDs, (2) various categories of HBAs, and (3) DESs incorporated with catalysts or additives. Moreover, the correlation between the Kamlet-Taft parameters of DESs and the efficiency of lignin extraction is reviewed. Finally, the structural transformations of lignin under different DES pretreatment conditions are systematically discussed, and viewpoints on the opportunities and challenges for green and efficient lignin extraction according to existing problems are also given. Lignin extraction and chemical transformations in DESs are shown in Fig. 2. ## 2 Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) DESs are eutectic mixtures generally consisting of a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) and a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA), which combine _via_ hydrogen bond (H-bond) interactions.39,40 H-bonds within the mixtures are responsible for charge delocalization; thus, the melting point of DESs is much lower than that of the individual components.41 For example, the mixture of ChCl (m.p. 302 °C) with urea (m.p. 132 °C) can lead to DESs with a melting point of 12 °C.42 DESs possess many merits, including the availability of raw materials, easy synthesis, tunable physicochemical properties, and good recyclability.43 DESs have been synthesized and used in different applications, such as catalysis, pharmaceutical applications, and biomass processing.44 Generally, DESs are classified into four main categories based on the nature of the complexing agent (Fig. 3). Type I DESs are formed from metal halides (e.g., AlCl3, AgCl, and CuCl3) and quaternary ammonium salts (e.g., choline chloride (ChCl), and have not been significantly applied to ligno-cellulose processing owing to the high melting points of non-hydrated metal halides.39 Type II DESs mainly include hydrated metal halides (e.g., AlCl3.6H2O) and ChCl, which are more viable for industrial processes because most of these chemicals are low cost and are inherently insensitive to air/moisture. Type III DESs mainly consist of ChCl and various HBDs, such as carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amides. Type IV DESs include inorganic transition metals and HBDs (e.g., urea), even though metal salts do not normally ionize in non-aqueous media.45 Among the four types of DESs, Type III is the most common (especially in biomass processing), due to their low-cost starting materials, easy preparation, interactivity with water, low viscosity, and high biodegradability.37,46 The solvent properties greatly influence the efficiency of biomass pretreatment, delignification capability, and struc- tural change of lignin. The important properties of DESs include the melting point, viscosity, conductivity, density, polarity, and surface tension. One of the important features of DESs is that they possess a lower melting point than their individual con- stituents, which is responsible for the charge delocalization due to the formation of H-bonds between HBAs and HBDs.39 Hence, most DESs with low melting points exist as liquids at room temperature, allowing them to be used as solvents in biomass processing. In general, the melting point of DESS decreases upon increasing the H-bonding strength between mixtures.47 However, the presence of extensive H-bonding net- works within a mixture may increase the viscosity of DESS. Numerous studies have revealed that DESs with high viscos- ities are unfavorable for lignin extraction due to the low rates of heat and mass transfer during DES pretreatment.⁴³ The high viscosity of DESS still poses a problem. Conductivity and surface tension are closely related to viscosity. 43,48 It has been reported that reducing the viscosity of DESs can promote its conductivity. 49 Moreover, the conduc- tivity of DESs is inversely proportional to temperature. 50 In most cases, DESs have higher surface tensions than many con- ventional ILs.51 The presence of water and low temperature can enhance the surface tension of DESS. 52 The surface tension of DESs strongly depends on the intermolecular forces between mixtures; thus, highly viscous DESs are fluids with high surface tensions. 53 Density also is an important property of DESs, as it can reveal the activity and molecular mobility of the solution. This information is helpful in some applications like lignin extraction processes. In most cases, DESs have a higher density than water. 37,53 It is generally observed that increasing the temperature or adding water to DESs lowers their density. 53-55 Overall, the understanding of the prepa- ration, classification, and physiochemical properties of DESS facilitate their utilization in lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin extraction. ## 3 The effect of the structure– function relationships of DESs on lignin extraction The most important step during lignin valorization is the efficient extraction/dissolution of lignin with favorable pro- perties. Among these factors, the quality and quantity of functional group in DES com- ponents have the greatest influence. The DESs are usually pre- pared by mixing natural and renewable constituents, which determines the properties of the synthetic DESs and their be- havior during lignin fractionation from biomass. 3.1 Functional group type and number in HBDs Many HBDs including carboxylic acids, polyols, and amides are suitable for DES synthesis. The functional group of HBDs can interact with lignin, which affects the lignin extraction efficiency and chemical structure. Investigating the relationships between the types of functional groups in HBDs and lignin extraction is important to produce DESs to extract lignin with tailored properties. In addition, depending on the number of functional groups (e.g., carboxyl groups) in HBDs, the lignin extraction yield has been reported to vary (Fig. 4). 3.1.1 Carboxyl-containing HBDs. To further understand the influence of various carboxyl-con- taining HBDs on the performance of DESs, it is necessary to explore the structure-function relationships of various car- boxyl-containing DESs. The properties of carboxylic acid-based HBDs can affect the performance of DESs during lignin extraction. Previous research has shown that the lignin extraction ability improves with the acid strength of HBD. The acid dissociation constant (pKa) of monocarboxylic acid-based DESs increases in the order: ChCl/formic acid, ChCl/lactic acid, ChCl/acetic acid, ChCl/butanoic acid, and ChCl/propionic acid, while the lignin extraction performance generally decreases. 59 However, ChCl/ lactic acid (pKa = 3.86) produced a greater pretreatment effect than a stronger acid, ChCl/malonic (pKa₁ = 2.83, pKa₂ = 5.69).63 However, ChCl/malonic acid exhibited a better deligni- fication performance from rice straw than ChCl/oxalic acid (pKa₁ = 1.25, pKa₂ = 4.14).60 These results implied that the lignin fractionation efficiency was not necessarily related to the amount or strength of the acid when the HBD contained more than one carboxyl group. The number of carboxyl groups in an HBD is positively correlated with the extent of delignification during DES pretreatment. ChCl/lactic acid (1:9 molar ratio) (a monocarboxylic acid) is capable of selectively dissolving 95% of lignin from poplar and achieving higher lignin extraction yield than ChCl/succinic acid (a dicarboxylic acid) and ChCl/citric acid (a tricarboxylic acid).65 The result indicated that the monocarboxylic acid HBD possessed the optimal extraction capacity compared with the di- and tricarboxylic acids. This finding agrees well with Tan et al., who showed that the lignin extraction efficiency declined as follows: ChCl/lactic acid > ChCl/malic acid > ChCl/citric acid at the same molar ratio.59 One possible explanation for the weak delignification of di- and tricarboxylic acids is that the carboxyl groups in the HBD may easily be activated and thus release carbon dioxide at relatively high temperatures.63 The study also found that extra carboxyl groups in HBDs formed more H-bonds and extensive dimer chains, which reduced the mass transfer rate of the solvent system.66 This implied that efficient interactions between DESs and lignins were impaired when there was more than one carboxyl group in the HBD. Hence, the number of carboxyl groups in HBDs is inversely proportional to the delignification ability of the DESs. 3.1.2 Hydroxyl-containing HBDs. HBDs with hydroxyl groups are also widely used to synthesize DESs, including poly-alcohol-based HBDs (e.g., ethylene glycol, propylene glycol, and glycerol) and carbohydrate-based HBDs (e.g., glucose, fructose, and xylitol).67,68 This type of DES usually exhibits good biocompatibility with enzymes and microorganisms at near-neutral pH when mixed with a nontoxic HBA (e.g., betaine, ChCl). Compared with the performance of DESs with the same number of carboxyl groups, ChCl/lactic acid (C3H6O3) with a 33.5% lignin yield outperformed ChCl/propionic acid (C3H6O2) with 20.4% and ChCl/malic acid (C4H6O5) achieved a higher lignin yield (22%) than ChCl/succinic acid (C4H6O4) (6%). 59 Therefore, the presence of hydroxyl groups in HBDs improves the performance of DESs during lignin extraction, due to interactions between the hydroxyl groups in the HBD and the free and etherified hydroxyl groups in lignin. Therefore, exploring how the hydroxyl groups in HBDs affect the performance of DESs will help improve pretreatment by DESs. The number of hydroxyl groups in HBDs is inversely corre-lated with lignin removal. ChCl/glycerol showed worse lignin extractability than ChCl/ethylene glycol. 63,65 In another work, the pretreatment efficiency and lignin removability of polyalco-hol-based DESs decreased in the order of ethylene glycol > gly-cerol > xylitol for polyol sequences when using lactic acid as the HBA. 60 Therefore, during DES pretreatment, a lower delignification rate was associated with a higher number of hydroxyl groups in the HBD. It was deduced that the extra hydroxyl groups in HBDs formed an extensive H-bond network between HBAs and HBDs, thus weakening the ability of the HBA to compete with intra-molecular bonding in the biomass components.71 With the same number of hydroxyl groups in different positions, the delignification ability was also slightly different. For example, ChCl/1,3-propanediol separated more lignin from rice straw than ChCl/1,2-propanediol. 60 The author showed that the greater hydrophobicity of 1,3-propanediol-based DESs promoted lignin extraction using the hydrophobic phenylpropanoid skeleton. 3.1.3 Amine/amide-containing HBDs. To further under- stand the effect of functional groups in HBDs on the perform- ance of DESS, HBDs with amine/amide groups, such as urea, imidazole, and ethanolamine, were explored for their lignin fractionation effects. For instance, corncob pretreated by ChCl/ imidazole at 150 °C removed 88% of lignin.72 Amines or amides present in HBDs improved lignin extraction by DESS, due to the loosened linkages between lignin and carbo- hydrates. A common feature of amine/amide-based DESs is their basicity, which is conducive for the extraction of lignin from lignocellulose. As the basicity decreased from ChCl/ monoethanolamine, ChCl/diethanolamine, ChCl/ N-methyldiethanolamine, to ChCl/urea, the lignin removal rate significantly decreased from 81.0%, 73.5%, 44.6%, to 27.7%, respectively.73 The main reason for this trend was that the phe- nolic hydroxyl groups of lignin were deprotonated in alkaline solutions. In addition, the effect of the number of amine groups in the HBD on the lignin removal ability was also inves- tigated to improve pretreatment efficiency. Lactic acid/forma- mide achieved a higher lignin removal rate from rice straw than lactic acid/urea,60 which implied that the pretreatment performance of amine/amide-based HBDs showed an identical trend to hydroxyl-containing HBDs. HBDs with extra amines/ amides or hydroxyls can form more intermolecular H-bonds with HBAs, which reduces the number of free and active groups capable of interacting with lignocellulose and lowers the lignin production efficiency during DES pretreatment. 3.1.4 Alkyl chain length of HBD. Few investigations have been conducted on the relationship between the aliphatic chain length and lignin extractability, although initial research suggests that the alkyl group position in the HBD appears to affect the lignin extraction efficiency. Methyldiethanolamine (44.6%) containing an alkyl group (methyl) showed a weaker lignin fractionation ability than diethanolamine (73.5%).73 The main cause was the likely steric hindrance from the methyl group in methyldiethanolamine, which hampered the lignin fractionation efficiency. Moreover, the alkyl chain length of the HBD also influences lignin extraction. For monocarboxylic HBDs, the extracted lignin yield decreased as follows: ChCl/formic acid (62%) > ChCl/acetic acid (27%) > ChCl/propionic acid (20%) > ChCl/butanoic acid (14%) (Fig. 5).59 For dicarboxylic HBDs, the lignin extraction rate decreased as follows: ChCl/oxalic acid (98.5%) > ChCl/malonic acid (56.5%) > ChCl/glutaric acid (34.3%).63 Overall, HBDs containing shorter alkyl chains were more effective at delignification than those with longer chains, possibly due to electron donation from the alkyl group to the oxygen of the -OH group in the acid, which intensified the H-bonding strength.74 Weaker acids ionize to a lesser extent; therefore, decreasing the chain length of the HBD will increase the ability of the solvent to donate protons, which improves the DES pretreatment performance. However, another research study has found that ChCl/lactic acid (C3H6O3) produced a higher delignification efficiency than ChCl/glycolic acid (C2H4O3) when pretreated under the same conditions.60 It is likely that intramolecular H-bonds between adjacent functional groups in glycolic acid formed more easily than those in lactic acid, which made it difficult to cleave the various bonds in lignin. Numerous lignin-derived phenolic compounds, such as resorcinol, vanillin, and catechol, have been evaluated as HBDs for synthesizing DESs in biomass pretreatment. Kim et al. tested ten lignin-derived phenolic compounds as HBDs to prepare novel DESs, and only four phenolic-based HBDs (4-hydroxybenzyl alcohol, catechol, vanillin (VAN), and p-coumaric acid (PCA)) formed a homogeneous solvent with ChCl.75 The authors revealed that HBDs with methoxyl groups at the *ortho* position (G unit and S unit) synthesized almost no DESs compared with those without methoxyl groups due to the steric hindrance of the methoxyl groups adjacent to the hydroxyl groups. Among the four DESs, ChCl/PCA at 160 °C for 3 h achieved the highest lignin removal rate (60.8%), followed by ChCl/vanillin (52.5%), ChCl/catechol (49.0%), and ChCl/4-hydroxybenzyl alcohol (0.4%). The lignin extraction performance of ChCl/ formic acid was compared with that of pure formic acid, and the results showed that ChCl/formic acid removed 40.7% of lignin, while pure formic acid only removed 9.0% from herbal residues. 79 Hence, the DESs display better lignin fractionation than the corresponding acids alone. The chemical properties of DESs can be described by the Kamlet–Taft (K–T) solvatochromic parameters, which serve as a quantitative tool.⁹⁹ The K–T parameters are defined by three solvent parameters, including H-bond-donating ability (α), H-bond-accepting ability (β), and polarizability (π*). These parameters can be used to explain the internal connections between DES properties and their ability to fractionate lignin from lignocellulose.²³ For example, Yu et al. studied the correlations between the K–T parameters of DESs and the lignin extraction rate and found that the β value was positively correlated with the delignification rate.⁷¹ The authors explained that a high H-bond basicity improved the ability of the DES to break the H-bond network in lignin. In another work, ChCl/oxalic acid with a high H-bond acidity (α = 1.31) broke the structure of the lignin–hemicellulose complex, while ChCl/urea and ChCl/glycerol did not.²⁸ This is because the acidic protons dissociated from DESs catalyzed the cleavage of ethers and esters in lignocellulose. Moreover, the lignin-dissolving ability was related to the difference between the values of α and β (α–β), which shows a net H-bond-donating ability of DESs. For example, the lignin solubility/extraction capability of DESs increased at higher α–β values.⁸⁵,¹⁰⁰ These results imply that DESs with high α–β values could form strong H-bonds with lignin, which was favorable for the degradation of lignin. In addition to α and β values, the π* value of DESs also affects the lignin extraction ability. For ChCl-based DESs, chloride anions are capable of forming strong H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups of lignin fragments, which break the intramolecular H-bond network of lignin and promote lignin fractionation.71 C-H···π and O···H bonding interactions contributed to the high interaction energy between ChCl/lactic acid and lignin, thus enhancing lignin dissolution in DESs.102 An insight into the structural transformations of lignin during DES pretreatment is not only essential to understand and overcome biomass recalcitrance but it is also pivotal to design optimal pathways for lignin valorization. During DES processing, both depolymerization and repolymerization can occur; thus, the final structure of the DES-extracted lignin may be the net effect of the two reactions whose outcome strongly depends on the processing method, which includes: (1) acidic DES pretreatment, (2) alkaline DES pretreatment, and (3) neutral DES pretreatment. This following section summarizes the possible chemical reactions during DES pretreatment, with a focus on the fate of β-O-4' linkages in the lignin substructure. ## 5.1 Acidic DES pretreatment Acidic DESs exhibit excellent performance during lignin extraction; thus, investigation into the structural transformations of lignin in acidic DESs is necessary for lignin valorization. The possible reactions of the lignin substructure during acidic DES pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 10. The main reaction is lignin depolymerization, especially the breakage of β-O-4' bonds. Alvarez-Vasco et al. have reported that when treated with ChCl/lactic acid, guaiacylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (a β-O-4' bond lignin dimeric model compound) got converted into guaiacol and Hibbert's ketone.²³ This result demonstrated that the breakage of β-O-4' bonds favored lignin depolymerization, which consequently facilitated lignin fractionation from lignocellulose. Similar research also proved that acidic DESs can selectively cleave ethers and degrade a small portion of C-C bonds (e.g., β-5' and β-β') in lignin, which facilitates lignin separation from lignocellulose.⁶⁵,¹⁰³ The prevailing depolymerization pathway during acidic DESs is the destruction of the β-O-4' linkages among phenylpropane units via mild acid-catalyzed bond cleavage.²³,³⁴,¹⁰⁰,¹⁰⁴ The most important step is the protonation of the α-OH group to form a stable benzylic carbocation. Then, the benzylic carbocation loses the terminal γ-CH₂OH group to generate α-β unsaturated compounds and formaldehyde, which further promotes the cleavage of ether bonds (Route I). Although a variety of DESs has been widely studied and used in biomass pretreatment, there is still a need for a rigorous investigation on the structure-function relationship of DESs during processing to increase the pretreatment efficiency. The properties of ideal DESs for lignin extraction are still unclear. Research on DES synthesis and its practical applications are still in their infancy, and thus more in-depth studies are required to increase DES pretreatment efficiency in future works. To achieve the ultimate goal of efficient lignin extraction and upgrading in terms of depolymerization and functionalization, there is still much work to do, as follows: (1) DESs are ideal solvents for lignin fractionation and cata-lytic upgrading. Nevertheless, most DES screening methods are based on time-consuming trial and error. The directed design of DESs based on their intended purpose is promising. Besides, if lignin-derived compounds can be further used to synthesize DESs, a promising approach may be opened up to utilize lignin. Type III DESs mainly consist of ChCl and various HBDs, such as carboxylic acids, alcohols, and amides. The important properties of DESs include the melting point, viscosity, conductivity, density, polarity, and surface tension. One of the important features of DESs is that they possess a lower melting point than their individual con- stituents, which is responsible for the charge delocalization due to the formation of H-bonds between HBAs and HBDs.39 Hence, most DESs with low melting points exist as liquids at room temperature, allowing them to be used as solvents in biomass processing. In general, the melting point of DESS decreases upon increasing the H-bonding strength between mixtures.47 However, the presence of extensive H-bonding net- works within a mixture may increase the viscosity of DESS. Numerous studies have revealed that DESs with high viscos- ities are unfavorable for lignin extraction due to the low rates of heat and mass transfer during DES pretreatment.⁴³ The high viscosity of DESS still poses a problem. Conductivity and surface tension are closely related to viscosity. 43,48 It has been reported that reducing the viscosity of DESs can promote its conductivity. 49 Moreover, the conduc- tivity of DESs is inversely proportional to temperature. 50 In most cases, DESs have higher surface tensions than many con- ventional ILs.51 The presence of water and low temperature can enhance the surface tension of DESS. 52 The surface tension of DESs strongly depends on the intermolecular forces between mixtures; thus, highly viscous DESs are fluids with high surface tensions. 53 Density also is an important property of DESs, as it can reveal the activity and molecular mobility of the solution. This information is helpful in some applications like lignin extraction processes. In most cases, DESs have a higher density than water. 37,53 It is generally observed that increasing the temperature or adding water to DESs lowers their density. 53-55 Overall, the understanding of the prepa- ration, classification, and physiochemical properties of DESS facilitate their utilization in lignocellulose pretreatment and lignin extraction. ## 3 The effect of the structure– function relationships of DESs on lignin extraction The most important step during lignin valorization is the efficient extraction/dissolution of lignin with favorable pro- perties. The chemical properties of DESs can be described by the Kamlet–Taft (K–T) solvatochromic parameters, which serve as a quantitative tool.⁹⁹ The K–T parameters are defined by three solvent parameters, including H-bond-donating ability (α), H-bond-accepting ability (β), and polarizability (π*). These parameters can be used to explain the internal connections between DES properties and their ability to fractionate lignin from lignocellulose.²³ For example, Yu et al. studied the correlations between the K–T parameters of DESs and the lignin extraction rate and found that the β value was positively correlated with the delignification rate.⁷¹ The authors explained that a high H-bond basicity improved the ability of the DES to break the H-bond network in lignin. In another work, ChCl/oxalic acid with a high H-bond acidity (α = 1.31) broke the structure of the lignin–hemicellulose complex, while ChCl/urea and ChCl/glycerol did not.²⁸ This is because the acidic protons dissociated from DESs catalyzed the cleavage of ethers and esters in lignocellulose. Moreover, the lignin-dissolving ability was related to the difference between the values of α and β (α–β), which shows a net H-bond-donating ability of DESs. For example, the lignin solubility/extraction capability of DESs increased at higher α–β values.⁸⁵,¹⁰⁰ These results imply that DESs with high α–β values could form strong H-bonds with lignin, which was favorable for the degradation of lignin. In addition to α and β values, the π* value of DESs also affects the lignin extraction ability. For ChCl-based DESs, chloride anions are capable of forming strong H-bonds with the hydroxyl groups of lignin fragments, which break the intramolecular H-bond network of lignin and promote lignin fractionation.71 C-H···π and O···H bonding interactions contributed to the high interaction energy between ChCl/lactic acid and lignin, thus enhancing lignin dissolution in DESs.102 An insight into the structural transformations of lignin during DES pretreatment is not only essential to understand and overcome biomass recalcitrance but it is also pivotal to design optimal pathways for lignin valorization. During DES processing, both depolymerization and repolymerization can occur; thus, the final structure of the DES-extracted lignin may be the net effect of the two reactions whose outcome strongly depends on the processing method, which includes: (1) acidic DES pretreatment, (2) alkaline DES pretreatment, and (3) neutral DES pretreatment. This following section summarizes the possible chemical reactions during DES pretreatment, with a focus on the fate of β-O-4' linkages in the lignin substructure. ## 5.1 Acidic DES pretreatment Acidic DESs exhibit excellent performance during lignin extraction; thus, investigation into the structural transformations of lignin in acidic DESs is necessary for lignin valorization. The possible reactions of the lignin substructure during acidic DES pretreatment are illustrated in Fig. 10. The main reaction is lignin depolymerization, especially the breakage of β-O-4' bonds. Alvarez-Vasco et al. have reported that when treated with ChCl/lactic acid, guaiacylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (a β-O-4' bond lignin dimeric model compound) got converted into guaiacol and Hibbert's ketone.²³ This result demonstrated that the breakage of β-O-4' bonds favored lignin depolymerization, which consequently facilitated lignin fractionation from lignocellulose. Similar research also proved that acidic DESs can selectively cleave ethers and degrade a small portion of C-C bonds (e.g., β-5' and β-β') in lignin, which facilitates lignin separation from lignocellulose.⁶⁵,¹⁰³ The prevailing depolymerization pathway during acidic DESs is the destruction of the β-O-4' linkages among phenylpropane units via mild acid-catalyzed bond cleavage.²³,³⁴,¹⁰⁰,¹⁰⁴ The most important step is the protonation of the α-OH group to form a stable benzylic carbocation. Then, the benzylic carbocation loses the terminal γ-CH₂OH group to generate α-β unsaturated compounds and formaldehyde, which further promotes the cleavage of ether bonds (Route I). For example, Shen and co-workers found that the chemical shift of the guaiacyl unit of lignin changed after ChCl/lactic acid pro- cessing, which suggested the formation of new C–C bonds via acid-catalyzed recondensation. 109,110 Repolymerization com- monly occurs through the formation of covalent bonds between the α-C of the benzylic carbocation and electron-rich positions on aromatic rings to obtain diphenylmethane com- pounds. However, the coupling between the electrophilic posi- tions on the aromatic rings of benzylic carbocations and elec- tron-rich positions of aromatic rings forms biphenyl com- pounds. Acidic DESs not only result in the condensation of lignin fraction (e.g. ChCl/lactic acid) but also preserve lignin from condensation and produce non-condensed lignin (e.g., ChCl/boric acid). Non-condensed lignin was reported by Hiltunen's groups, with softwood sawdust as the raw material and ChCl/boric acid as the pretreatment solvent at 95 °C.111 The reason for the production of non-condensation lignin is that boric acid, a Lewis acid, can form esters with side-chain hydroxyl groups in lignin, thus reducing oligomerization and repolymerization reactions. In certain acidic DES systems, esterification occurs between carboxyl groups in acidic DESs and y-OH in lignin substruc- tures. Several research groups have reported that y-acetylated signals in DES-extracted lignin were observed by 2D-HSQC NMR (Fig. S1†), which indicated the acylation of lactic acid during ChCl/lactic acid pretreatment. 65,82,100,109 In addition to the above reactions, demethoxylation and dehydration also fre- quently occur during DES pretreatment. 100,110 However, the exact mechanism is complex and not clearly understood. ## 5.2 Alkaline DES pretreatment Alkaline solvents are often used to extract lignin from biomass because lignin is an alkaline-soluble biopolymer.107 For example, chemical fractions of holocellulose, α-cellulose, and acid-insoluble lignin were pretreated with ChCl/urea, and lignin exhibited a higher selective solubility compared with other chemical fractions.112 Alkaline DES pretreatment destroys lignin-carbohydrate compounds, disrupts lignin by breaking the ether bonds, and eventually results in lignin depolymerization/repolymerization.97 Similarly, pretreatment with basic ILs resulted in the cleavage of ether bonds, along with demethoxylation, dehydration, and repolymerization primarily through β-β'and β-5' linkages.113 In another study, basic 7228 | Green Chem., 2020, 22, 7219-7232 This journal is  The Royal Society of Chemistry 2020 Published on 22 September 2020. Yu et al. revealed that the intramolecular H-bonds in ChCl/glycerol were mutually constrained by anionic H-bonds ([Cl(glycerol)]⁻) and cationic H-bonds ([Ch(glycerol)]⁺), in which ChCl/glycerol had weakly competing interactions towards the linkages in the network of the lignin-carbohydrate complex.⁷¹ Wan and co-workers showed that lignin recovered from ChCl/glycerol pretreatment partially preserved the β-O-4' linkages and had a similar structure to protolignin.⁶⁹ In another study, the lignin extracted after ChCl/ethylene glycol pretreatment exhibited a low molecular weight and preserved partial β-O-4' bonds;⁸⁷,¹¹⁶ however, few studies have examined the lignin transformation mechanism using alkaline DESs. However, a comprehensive study of the structural transformation of lignin in neutral DES systems is required. # 6 Conclusions and prospects The applications of DESs for lignin extraction and conversion have been widely recognized. Although a variety of DESs has been widely studied and used in biomass pretreatment, there is still a need for a rigorous investigation on the structure-function relationship of DESs during processing to increase the pretreatment efficiency. The properties of ideal DESs for lignin extraction are still unclear. Research on DES synthesis and its practical applications are still in their infancy, and thus more in-depth studies are required to increase DES pretreatment efficiency in future works. To achieve the ultimate goal of efficient lignin extraction and upgrading in terms of depolymerization and functionalization, there is still much work to do, as follows: (1) DESs are ideal solvents for lignin fractionation and cata-lytic upgrading. Nevertheless, most DES screening methods are based on time-consuming trial and error. The directed design of DESs based on their intended purpose is promising. Besides, if lignin-derived compounds can be further used to synthesize DESs, a promising approach may be opened up to utilize lignin.
